title: No Country for Tech Bros | The Point Magazine
gist: A reported account of Balaji Srinivasan's Network State Conference in Singapore and his Network School on Malaysia's failed Forest City development, arguing that the network-state movement has pivoted from digital 'cloud countries' to buying distressed physical real estate, is financed by crypto wealth and Thiel-backed Pronomos Capital, and is simultaneously bidding for US Freedom Cities policy. The Network School's Malaysian license was revoked on July 21st and it relocated to Kazakhstan, illustrating that host-state permission, not technology, is the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Network states have moved from fringe pipe dream to a tertiary MAGA policy priority under Trump's second term, with insiders drafting Freedom Cities proposals and chartering jets to Mar-a-Lago.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Special-economic-zone enabling legislation is a live US policy catalyst; watch for land-designation and charter-city bills as an option on real-estate, crypto and defense-adjacent developers.
insights.quote: Network-state insiders were drafting Freedom Cities proposals and flying in chartered jets to Mar-a-Lago.
insights.locator: In the months leading up to the conference

insights.claim: Próspera's head of growth expected Freedom Cities legislation to be drafted by the end of the year and considered its passage effectively certain.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term legislative timeline to test; slippage past year-end would falsify the movement's most bankable claim on Washington.
insights.quote: “We’re hoping to have legislation drafted by the end of the year,” Próspera’s head of growth told me when we met in Austin.
insights.locator: In the months leading up to the conference

insights.claim: US foreign policy is being used to protect private charter-city investments: the Trump administration backed a right-wing candidate in Honduras's election seemingly to defend Próspera, a Peter Thiel-backed zone locked in litigation with the Honduran government.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Political risk on charter-city assets is now partly hedged by US diplomatic muscle, which cuts both ways if an administration changes.
insights.locator: Próspera, a charter city backed by Peter Thiel

insights.claim: The network-state strategy is explicitly to 'exit' the American-led order and simultaneously 'enter' its power structure, using Trump as an ideological laundering mechanism for techno-accelerationism.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Treat secessionist rhetoric as a negotiating posture, not a retreat; these actors are bidding for state contracts and legal carve-outs at the same time they claim to be leaving.
insights.quote: The plan is to both “exit” the American-led order and “enter” its power structure at the same time.
insights.locator: One answer was the special economic zones

insights.claim: Forest City, the Malaysian island development hosting Balaji Srinivasan's Network School, is a failed $100 billion, twenty-year Chinese-Malaysian project that had drawn only about 10,000 residents against an original 700,000 target after roughly $5 billion was spent.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The flagship physical node of the network-state movement sits on an asset that missed its occupancy target by ~99%; underwriting any zone on 'build it and they will come' demand should be discounted accordingly.
insights.quote: By 2025, with close to five billion dollars already spent on apartment towers and McMansions, only ten thousand people had actually moved there—a little over one percent of the initial target.
insights.locator: The school was on a man-made island

insights.claim: Malaysia rescued Forest City by rebranding it a 'special financial zone' with a 5 percent corporate tax rate and tax-free family offices, and Srinivasan moved 128 resident students in the same month, September 2024.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Tax-arbitrage terms, not demand, are what pull capital and residents into these zones — the binding variable to track is the statutory rate and family-office treatment, not the marketing.
insights.quote: dropping the corporate tax rate to 5 percent and allowing family offices to operate tax-free
insights.locator: In a bid to save the project

insights.claim: Srinivasan reframed the Network School's core business as turning around distressed real estate, telling students 'our core competency will be turning around distressed real estate' and restructuring them into a volunteer labor tier of one, ten or a hundred hours a week.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The actual monetizable model here is buying stranded property cheap and importing a captive community to reprice it — comparable to Adam Neumann's Flow, and dependent on free or near-free labor.
insights.quote: “We are rebooting the community as a tech tribe,” Srinivasan said to start the meeting, “and our core competency will be turning around distressed real estate.”
insights.locator: Four days after the first town hall

insights.claim: A Network School student described the venture's model as Adam Neumann's Flow — 'WeWork plus apartments plus amenities in a single building' — organized as a multitiered hierarchy where full-time workers are called 'generals' who joke about receiving fiefdoms.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The comparable for valuing network-state ventures is a co-living/co-working operator with cult economics, not a sovereign entity — and WeWork's history is the base rate.
insights.quote: “WeWork plus apartments plus amenities in a single building”—an integrated tech campus.
insights.locator: One of Srinivasan’s students later explained

themes.theme: Jurisdiction risk kills the physical node

insights.claim: The Iskander Puteri City Council revoked the Network School's business license effective the next day on July 21st and ordered it to cease operations, after a probe into whether it was hiding Israeli nationals; Srinivasan announced the same day that the school was moving to Kazakhstan.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Host-government revocation risk is the dominant risk in zone ventures and it can crystallize in 24 hours — size positions in charter-city exposure for total, sudden write-off.
insights.quote: the Iskander Puteri City Council announced it would revoke the Network School’s business license, effective the next day, and ordered it to cease operations.
insights.locator: In the end, though, it wasn’t the mold

insights.claim: Srinivasan's defense of the Network School leaned on sunk investment — claiming his companies had put more than RM100 million (about $25 million USD) into Malaysia — and on an implicit threat to relocate, which the government evidently read as a threat and answered by revoking the license.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Capital-flight threats are weak leverage against sovereign hosts; the exit-option rhetoric that attracts investors is precisely what provokes the counterparty that grants the license.
insights.locator: This was the outcome of a public imbroglio

insights.claim: The relocation to Kazakhstan can be read either as proof network states are doomed because culture is not fungible, or, per Patri Friedman, as vindication that physical geography is waning because there will always be another opportunistic state to deal with.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The bull-bear crux for the whole sector: if host jurisdictions are truly fungible, revocation is a rounding error; if not, each zone carries idiosyncratic sovereign risk that cannot be diversified away.
insights.quote: there will always be another state to make a deal with, another opportunistic leader who wants to attract global tech talent.
insights.locator: Maybe this proved that network states are doomed

insights.claim: The claim that corporate city-states will outperform democracies because they are consumer-focused is undercut by the fact that corporations degrade too — and in a city-state the resident has no political recourse, only terms of service.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The governance discount on privately run cities should widen, not narrow: exit rights are the only remedy, and they are worthless once you own the property.
insights.quote: “The logic of corporate city-states is that because they’re consumer-focused, they’ll perform better than democracies as service providers,” the student said. “But corporations are just as likely to become degraded.”
insights.locator: The mold situation, he observed

insights.claim: Homeowners are the maximally locked-in users of a corporate city-state, which makes enshittification more profitable there than on a software platform.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: If you buy property inside a privately governed zone you hold an asset whose operator has both the incentive and ability to extract from you; price that agency risk explicitly.
insights.quote: “What kind of user is more locked in than a homeowner?”
insights.locator: The mold situation, he observed

insights.claim: When a serious mold outbreak hit the Network School's converted hotel, Srinivasan's response was to dismiss it as 'a social contagion, like trans stuff', require NDAs, and force students to 'double opt in or opt out' rather than concede the defect.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Operator response to a physical defect is the cleanest real-world test of private-governance quality, and this one failed it — a directly observable due-diligence marker for any such project.
insights.quote: “Look, I wouldn’t be here if I thought it was a big deal, okay? That’s the ultimate proof. I think it’s honestly a social contagion, like trans stuff.”
insights.locator: About a month after the school opened

themes.theme: The demand side is thinner than claimed

insights.claim: The movement's business model treats digital nomads as the market and network states as the service providers, but attendees were repeating an incorrect figure of over forty million digital nomads as the basis for that demand.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The addressable-market number underpinning zone development is inflated; supply of nodes in Belize, Panama and elsewhere is being built against a demand estimate nobody has verified.
insights.quote: people explained confidently—and incorrectly—that there are over forty million digital nomads in the world
insights.locator: According to this model, digital nomads were the market

insights.claim: Most crypto attendees at the Network State Conference had actually come to Singapore for TOKEN2049 and, when asked about network states, offered little more than 'it's pretty cool'.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Headline attendance figures for ideological conferences are borrowed from adjacent crypto events; treat claimed community size as a marketing artifact rather than evidence of conviction.
insights.locator: I’d come to the conference hoping to speak with impassioned ideologues

insights.claim: Network School capacity was about 250 people with an aspiration to reach a thousand, while applicants — mostly crypto workers and digital nomads — formed a backlog in the thousands.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Scale here is measured in hundreds, not city-sized populations; any thesis that these become meaningful jurisdictions needs two or three orders of magnitude of growth.
insights.quote: Currently, there were about 250 people at the school, Steger explained, with hopes to expand to a thousand.
insights.locator: Currently, there were about 250 people at the school

themes.theme: Crypto capital as the movement's balance sheet

insights.claim: Crypto's market capitalization briefly hit an all-time high of $4 trillion, and a widely circulated report framed it as a 'country' with 36 billionaires and 241,700 millionaires — the constituency Srinivasan is positioning himself to govern.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The network-state project is a wealth-management and jurisdiction-shopping play for crypto's newly rich; its funding cycle tracks crypto market cap, so a drawdown starves the zones.
insights.quote: This was a “country” with 36 billionaires and 241,700 millionaires, as a report making the rounds in crypto stated.
insights.locator: I was reminded of a factoid

insights.claim: The operative investor mantra on stage was Arthur Hayes's 'get your Bitcoin and get out' — convert fiat into Bitcoin, gold or great equities in anticipation of unchecked money printing, then relocate to a jurisdiction like Singapore or Dubai.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: This is a debasement trade coupled with a residency trade; the flow it implies is into hard assets plus low-tax hubs, not into domestic financial claims.
insights.quote: “take this fiat, however you can earn it, convert it to Bitcoin or gold or great equities, and then exit stage left.”
insights.locator: Hayes explained that his attitude came

insights.claim: Arthur Hayes and BitMEX, convicted of Bank Secrecy Act violations and fined a hundred million dollars, both received federal pardons from Trump in 2025 — the first pardon ever granted to a corporation.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Regulatory legal risk in crypto is now partly political and reversible, which changes how to price enforcement overhangs on exchanges with administration ties.
insights.quote: In 2025, Hayes received a federal pardon from Trump, and so did the exchange—the first ever pardon granted to a corporation.
insights.locator: Onstage, Srinivasan sat down for a “fireside chat”

insights.claim: The Network School pays students in Bitcoin or USDC bounties for tasks like clipping Srinivasan's podcast or reviewing Peter Thiel's books, marketed under the slogan 'Anyone. Anywhere. $100k. Global meritocracy is here.'
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Stablecoin and Bitcoin micro-bounties are becoming the payroll rail for borderless communities — an early, concrete use case for on-chain labor markets.
insights.quote: “Anyone. Anywhere. $100k. Global meritocracy is here.”
insights.locator: Steger clarified why “earn”

themes.theme: Zone proliferation and the Singapore template

insights.claim: Patri Friedman's Thiel-backed VC firm Pronomos Capital has invested in all the major network-state projects from Próspera to Praxis, making it the central financing node of the sector.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: One fund concentrates the sector's equity exposure; its portfolio announcements are the best leading indicator of where the next zone gets chartered.
insights.locator: The grandson of the economist Milton Friedman

insights.claim: Friedman argues governments are bigger herd animals than venture capitalists, so one working zone triggers a domino effect of copycat zones, with his stated lifetime North Star being the share of world population, GDP and land area 'rezoned into 21st-century government'.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: If correct, zone adoption is reflexive and non-linear — the trade is on the second and third sovereign to copy, not the first; watch Global South governments announcing zone legislation in clusters.
insights.quote: “I sometimes joke that governments are even more herd animals than venture capitalists are,” Patri said.
insights.locator: “Is there some scarcity here?”

insights.claim: There is a real scarcity constraint on the zone model: a country contributing 10 percent of its land area to one zone cannot repeat the deal many times.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Early zone operators capture scarce sovereign concessions; later entrants face worse terms, which argues for first-mover value in charter-city equity.
insights.quote: “If it’s 10 percent of their land that’s being contributed, they can’t do that many more times,”
insights.locator: “Is there some scarcity here?”

insights.claim: China's special economic zones, begun in 1979 from Shenzhen to Fuzhou and widely credited by economists with driving Chinese ascendance, are the explicit template charter-city advocates want reproduced on American soil via Freedom Cities.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: US zone policy will be sold on the Shenzhen precedent; the political case is strong enough that domestic SEZ legislation is a plausible, underpriced policy path.
insights.locator: One answer was the special economic zones

insights.claim: Singapore functions as the tech right's proof-of-concept for the CEO-politician, with Lee Kuan Yew's blend of cultural authoritarianism and technocratic planning explicitly held up as the startup-city ideal.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The governance model being marketed to investors is authoritarian-technocratic, which shapes which jurisdictions will host these projects and which rights investors and residents actually get.
insights.locator: On the tech right, Singapore is often held up

themes.theme: Balaji's worldview: helix, tech Zionism, China realism

insights.claim: Srinivasan's geopolitical frame divides the future of power into three coalitions — NYT (the American establishment), CCP (the centralized Chinese state) and BTC (the global internet) — and holds that only these three have the scale to survive an already-commenced all-out digital struggle.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: A compact map for how crypto-aligned capital reads geopolitics; it predicts allocation away from US institutional assets and toward Bitcoin plus Asian jurisdictions.
insights.locator: The future of power, according to Srinivasan’s worldview

insights.claim: Srinivasan's theory of history is a corkscrew of unbundling and rebundling — CD to MP3 to Spotify playlist — in which technology is destiny and nations are now in the unbundling phase.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: A reusable model for reading any incumbent institution: ask whether it is currently being unbundled or rebundled, and who captures the rebundle.
insights.quote: The CD gets unbundled into the MP3, which gets rebundled into the Spotify playlist.
insights.locator: In The Network State, Srinivasan offers up

insights.claim: Srinivasan's pitch has shifted from digital-first 'cloud countries' materializing out of thin air, as he wrote in Wired in 2013, to the network state as a physical, discrete unit for remaking the geopolitical map.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The movement has converged on land and buildings, which means it now carries real-estate, construction and sovereign-permitting risk it previously claimed to have escaped.
insights.quote: “we may begin to see cloud towns, then cloud cities, and ultimately cloud countries materialize out of thin air.”
insights.locator: But something had changed from his original pitch

insights.claim: Blogger Noah Smith framed the network state as a 'new Hanseatic League' — a modern cross-border network of trading cities functioning as a unified trade bloc.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: If zones federate into a trade bloc rather than competing individually, the investable unit becomes the network's shared standards and payment rails, not any single city.
insights.quote: creating “a modern-day network of network cities” that would function like a unified trade bloc.
insights.locator: Onstage in a Substack t-shirt

insights.claim: Tomas Pueyo's framework holds that societies organize around the most efficient means of wielding violence, that printing, the heavy plow and gunpowder produced the centralized nation-state, and that the internet, cryptocurrency and English as lingua franca are now running that process in reverse.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: A testable decentralization thesis: if technology is genuinely weakening states, fiscal capacity and tax bases erode first — watch sovereign revenue collection, not rhetoric.
insights.quote: “All these technologies that used to make the state a bigger force now make it weaker”
insights.locator: A Substacker named Tomas Pueyo

insights.claim: Asked how network states would defend themselves, Srinivasan answered that China is by far the world's strongest military power, that one Chinese shipyard makes more ships than the entire US Navy combined, and that 'the U.S. can't fight China' — so network states must avoid the physical realm entirely.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: An influential Silicon Valley figure is publicly conceding hard-power primacy to China, which is causing visible discomfort in a tech world simultaneously winning US defense contracts — a fault line to watch in defense-tech alignment.
insights.quote: “So my view is: the U.S. can’t fight China.”
insights.locator: “If we want our network states to last thousands of years,”

insights.claim: Srinivasan markets the network state as 'tech Zionism', casting himself as a Theodor Herzl for the 'gray tribe' and treating Judaism as a social technology — while simultaneously framing technologists as a persecuted class facing ramping anti-tech violence.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: This grievance framing is the recruitment engine and also the political liability that triggered the Malaysian backlash — ideology here is directly load-bearing on operating licenses.
insights.quote: “Technology is a class,” Srinivasan wrote on X, and most of the violence in the twentieth century “was on the basis of class.”
insights.locator: I wondered if that’s what Srinivasan meant

themes.theme: China's building model as cautionary precedent

insights.claim: China's ghost cities stem from a 'state entrepreneurialism' model in which local governments, as monopoly lessors of 40-to-70-year land-use rights, borrowed heavily against a four-trillion-yuan (about $586 billion) post-2008 stimulus and were evaluated on short-term GDP, encouraging trophy projects.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: The same incentive structure — land monopolist plus short-horizon promoter plus cheap credit — recurs wherever zones are built on speculative demand; it is the diagnostic to apply to Freedom Cities.
insights.quote: because local politicians’ performance was evaluated on the basis of short-term GDP gains, the system encouraged investment in trophy projects
insights.locator: The result is a model some theorists call

insights.claim: Chinese urbanization partly absorbed the overbuild — 68 percent of China's population lived in cities by 2025 versus 50 percent in 2010, roughly 290 million more people — yet dozens of ghost cities still exist.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Even history's largest demand tailwind did not clear all speculative supply; zones without a state-directed migration program have no equivalent backstop.
insights.quote: By 2025, a reported 68 percent of China’s population was living in cities, up from 50 percent in 2010—or about 290 million more people.
insights.locator: But the other part is structural

insights.claim: Forest City failed for a different reason than domestic ghost cities: it was a Belt and Road-style offshore project by a Chinese developer that tanked once the CCP blocked citizens from moving funds offshore, with COVID following a couple of years later.
insights.speaker: Sam Venis
insights.so_what: Chinese capital-control policy, not local demand, is the swing factor for offshore Chinese-built developments — a reminder that these assets are hostage to Beijing's capital account stance.
insights.quote: But once the CCP started preventing its citizens from moving funds offshore, the project quickly tanked.
insights.locator: Forest City is somewhat different
